source.title: Do Post-Training Algorithms Actually Differ? A Controlled Study Across Model Scales Uncovers Scale-Dependent Ranking Inversions

page_placements.theme: Evaluation protocols change measured scaling and rankings

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: It reports downstream benchmark accuracy for post-trained Qwen 2.5 Instruct models across sizes and compares how results change with scale. This bears conceptually on downstream predictability, but it does not measure held-out pretraining loss or fit scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper mentions Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. as prior work, but reports no tests of pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute; no small-run loss extrapolation; no compute-optimal parameter/token allocation; no architecture-shape comparison; and no power-law fitting or fit-sensitivity analysis. The reported post-training accuracy sweeps bear on V6. Rows capture the reported GSM8K scale comparison and the aggregate MATH and general-domain results; results cited from other work are omitted.
record.test_reason: The study compares post-training algorithms (SFT, DPO, SimPO, KTO, GRPO variants and others) on off-the-shelf Qwen 2.5 Instruct checkpoints at 0.5B to 7B. It measures no pretraining loss and fits no power law. It does not vary parameters, tokens or compute itself. Its 'scale' finding concerns which post-training algorithm ranks best at each size, not whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale or pretraining loss. Kaplan and Hoffmann are cited only as related work. The base-model GSM8K scores at four sizes are incidental reference points: four models, strict-match confounded by formatting at 3B, no trend fitted. They do not amount to a test of V6, so the record's 'tests/T2' and its V6 labels are not justified.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also conclude that none of 20 DPO variants significantly beats vanilla DPO; only SimPO differs, and it is worse. They propose a hierarchy of leverage: scale (~50 pp) >> paradigm (~10 pp) >> online/offline (~9 pp) >> loss function (~1 pp). They attribute the 7B inversion largely to format compliance, and state that scaling-law studies characterize pretraining, not post-training.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates post-training algorithms and downstream accuracy across model sizes, rather than measuring held-out pretraining loss or fitting scaling-law curves.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported downstream accuracy and method ranking vary with model scale, task, and strict versus flexible answer extraction; 7B uses LoRA while the core comparison at or below 3B uses full fine-tuning, with a 3B LoRA factorial also reported.

fits_no_version.finding: Post-training algorithm rankings on GSM8K change with model size. SGRPO is best at 1.5B (58.0%), while SimPO goes from worst at 0.5B to 3B to best at 7B with LoRA (85.8%). The authors attribute this partly to format compliance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The relative benefit of post-training algorithms is stable across model scale (a claim this study challenges).

fits_no_version.finding: Base Instruct checkpoint GSM8K strict-match is non-monotonic in size: 19.56%, 31.16%, 10.69% and 75.82% at 0.5B, 1.5B, 3B and 7B. The 3B dip is a format artifact; flexible extraction gives 62.9%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream benchmark scores of off-the-shelf checkpoints track size, but depend on the answer-extraction metric.

fits_no_version.finding: Algorithm spread on the trained task (19.3 pp on GSM8K) collapses on MATH (0.54 pp) and on general-domain benchmarks (0.47 pp at 1.5B, 0.71 pp at 7B).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Post-training algorithm choice matters mainly within the training distribution.

record.problems: One model family (Qwen 2.5), scales up to 7B, and GSM8K-centered synthetic post-training data; SGRPO was not tested at 3B or 7B. The paper states 7B full fine-tuning was infeasible, so the scale comparison there is not fully separated from the training-method setup. It also reports a DistributedSampler seed-propagation bug affecting earlier supervised-learning runs, later corrected in seed-fix experiments. The accuracy results are downstream task measures, not pretraining-loss scaling evidence.
record.rows_left_out: No reported result relevant to V6 was left out. Pretraining loss, law-fit, architecture, and compute-allocation material is not reported as a study result bearing on the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss, no power-law fit in parameters, tokens or compute.
No power-law fit for fine-tuning or other regimes; post-training accuracy only.
No fitted or predicted relation between scale or pretraining loss and downstream accuracy. Off-the-shelf models are compared at four sizes without a trend analysis.

record.verdict_notes: The record's gate note itself says the study does no scaling-law testing, yet it marks the study 'tests/T2' and labels V6 'challenges'. That label rests on post-training ranking inversions, which are not V6's construct. The study's 7B models use LoRA while smaller scales mostly use full fine-tuning; the paper covers a single model family and one training dataset.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss or parameter/token/compute scaling is measured.
No small-run fit or prediction of larger-run loss is reported.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or optimal parameter/token split is measured.
No controlled architecture depth/width comparison at fixed parameter count.
No power-law test in other modalities, repeated-data settings, or fine-tuning/transfer loss regimes.

The paper reports downstream accuracy at several model sizes, but does not fit or test a forecast from pretraining loss, nor establish a quantitative predictive law. The scale sweep is limited to one model family and post-training setup.
No scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits are fitted or compared across parameter counting, schedules, datasets, or fitting methods.

relation.reason: Related Work cites Kaplan and Hoffmann as pretraining scaling-law studies; the experiments do not test or apply their laws.

tranche.reason: The study compares post-training algorithm performance and ranking stability across checkpoints. It neither tests a scaling-law form or predictive scaling relationship nor uses one as a tool.
